options: The Present Simple — even though we are talking about the future.
The future with will, because the meaning is about the future.
The Past Simple, because the condition has not happened yet.

steps.title: The first conditional
steps.html:
if + Present Simplewill / won’t / might + base form
If one person has a cold,half the office will have it by Friday.
If your handshake is too soft,people might think you are not interested.
If you refuse a handshake,people will probably think you are unfriendly.
If it doesn’t rain,we won’t need the umbrella.
What will you doif he offers you his hand?

Use the first conditional for a real, possible situation and its result: If it rains, we will stay in.

Never put will after if. Say If it rains, not if it will rain.

You can put either half first. If the if half comes first, use a comma: If it rains, we’ll stay in. / We’ll stay in if it rains.

Use might instead of will when the result is only possible: If you shake his hand, he might be surprised.

In the next lesson the same present-tense rule appears after when, as soon as and until.

steps.title: The rise and fall of the handshake
steps.html:
Two thousand years old, and still not decided.

Reading

The handshake is about two thousand years old. The usual explanation is that an open right hand showed you were not holding a weapon: if I show you my hand, you will know I am safe.

It has never been the only way to say hello. In Thailand people put their hands together at chest level. In parts of Tibet people used to stick out their tongue. In many countries people kiss two or three times, starting with the right cheek. Younger people bump fists. And in the last few years, touching at all has become a question rather than a habit.

The reason is germs. A handshake moves about ten times more bacteria than a fist bump. If one person in an office has a cold, and everybody shakes hands all morning, half the office will have it by Friday.

But the handshake is not only about health, and that is why it has not disappeared. It carries information. If your handshake is too soft, people might think you are not interested. If it is too tight and strong, in China or Turkey you will seem rude. If you refuse one completely, people will probably think you are unfriendly — even when you are only being careful.

So what happens next? Doctors say the safest greeting is no touch at all. Most people say that if we stop shaking hands, we will lose something we cannot easily replace. Both are right. That is why we are still deciding.
